newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan vows neutrality as Afghan war rages.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan vows neutrality as Afghan war rages.

text.p: Pakistan renewed its vow on Thursday to remain neutral in the raging factional conflict in neighbouring Afghanistan, but rejected the Kabul government's charges that it was helping the rebel Taleban Islamic militia.
"The Kabul government has made unfounded allegations of Pakistani interference," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said. "We reject these accusations with the contempt they deserve.
"We have had and will continue to observe total neutrality while we must maintain a close watch on the events as they develop," the spokesman told reporters.

"As far as our neutrality is concerned, we are repeatedly pointing out to all our friends that it is in our interest to have a government which controls all of Afghanistan, it does not matter which government it is," the official said.
He said a stable government in Kabul could only be formed when the all the forces in the conflict were able to understand they cannot conquer each other and arrive at a settlement.
"We believe that all factions -- at the moment there are three major ones -- (must) be involved in the central government of Afghanistan, otherwise they will not be stable," he added.
The official also denied Kabul's charge that seven Pakistani army officers were caught on board a Taleban transport plane that landed at an Afghan government military airbase on Tuesday.

"There is absolutely no truth in the allegation that Pakistan army officers have been on the Taleban plane landing at the Bagram airport while apparently on a flight between Herat and Kandahar," the spokesman said.
Taleban later confirmed that the plane had landed in Bagram, but said the plane had been hijacked.
Taleban sources said two Pakistani Islamic scholars and three of their associates were on the plane, returning from a visit to Herat at the invitation of a pupil of the group leader.
"The story that they were Pakistani ulema (scholars) is a possibility, but we are checking it out," the spokesman said.
Afghan government forces and the Taleban militia fought on around the capital Kabul on Thursday, ignoring a U.N. Security Council call for an immediate ceasefire.

The ceasefire appeal was announced after a meeting of the 15-nation Security Council in New York following a string of military successes for the radical Taleban that has brought it to the gates of Kabul.
The Taleban controls more than half of Afghanistan, which has seen continual fighting between Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops backing a communist government left in 1989.
